newsitem.title: USA: Government wins major court victory against Staples.
newsitem.headline: Government wins major court victory against Staples.

text.p: A federal judge Monday dealt a potentially fatal blow to the planned $4.6 billion merger of office superstore chains Staples Inc. and Office Depot Inc..
U.S. District Judge Thomas Hogan Hogan, in a preliminary injuction, ruled that the Federal Trade Commission had shown a "reasonable probability" the merger would substantially impair competition.
Following the ruling, Staples said it was likely to terminate the deal, which was launched 10 months ago.

"While we ardently disagree with the judge's decision, we respect the judicial process and it is likely we will discontinue our merger plans with Office Depot," Staples President Thomas Stemberg said in a statement.

Office Depot, in a separate statement, hinted it was taking a similar view. It said its core management team remained in place and that it would immediately begin to aggressively recruit people for open positions.
"The deal is dead. The companies will go their own ways and pursue their own strategies," said analyst Mark Mandel of The Chicago Corp.
Staples, the top player in the industry, is well positioned to compete without Office Depot, Mandel said.
"Clearly, Staples is in the driver's seat in the industry. They had the least to lose if the deal fell apart," he said.
"Office Depot has to rally its troops and get the fire back in its belly," he added.

A preliminary injunction prevents the merger until the case works its way through the courts, which could take a year or more. Under the law, the next step is for the FTC to conduct a months-long administrative trial on the merits of the merger.

Staples' Stemberg said last month that if Hogan granted the preliminary injunction, he would give up the costly court fight -- which cost the two firms more than $12 million -- and the merger would be dead.
The FTC argued successfully that the chains would likely have the power to raise consumer prices if they merged because office superstores are unique.
"We're delighted for consumers across America," said the FTC's Bill Baer, who heads the Bureau of Competition. "This transaction was fundamentally flawed."
Staples and Office Depot asserted they competed with everyone from Wal-Mart, which sells some office supplies, to CompUSA, which sells computers, as well as with mail-order supply firms.
Originally worth $4 billion, the proposed stock transaction had risen in value to about $4.6 billion, reflecting stock price fluctuations.

Market sources said Office Depot's stock price, which closed Monday at $19.4375 on the New York Stock Exchange, tumbled to about $14.50 in after-hours trading. Staples ended at $23.25, off 25 cents on Nasdaq.
Judge Hogan, appointed to the bench in the early 1980s by President Reagan, agreed with the government, based in part on his own visit to the superstores.
"Superstores are simply different in scale and appearance from other retailers," Hogan ruled, saying that was "evident to the court when visiting the various stores."

"No one entering a Wal-Mart would mistake it for an office superstore. No one entering Staples or Office Depot would mistakenly think he or she was in Best Buy or CompUSA. You certainly know an office superstore when you see one."

Hogan agreed that office products "are undeniably the same, no matters who sells them." But he said that although a firm can be a competitor in the overall marketplace, that "does not necessarily require that it be included in the relevant product market for antitrust purposes."
In this case, the special market was office supplies sold in office superstores.
The strength of emotion on both sides was evident as the parties emerged from the judge's chambers, where they picked up copies of the opinion.
"We won, we won," euphoric FTC staffers shouted as they came out the door. Baer restrained some, who were hugging and laughing with joy.

Next out was Staples' lead lawyer, who walked straight over to the FTC group and congratulated the lead attorney for the governent, George Cary. Looking grim, the attorney and the other lawyers for the companies left by a side door to the courthouse.

The attorneys general of New York, California, Illinois, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Ohio, Virginia and North Carolina had also weighed in with a brief opposing the merger, arguing the main issue was whether competition would be protected.
The judge's ruling reverberated outside the orbit of Staples and Office Depot.

"It's going to give others pause," said Kevin Arquit, an antitrust attorney with Rogers & Wells in New York. "It shows that retailing is no different from any other area in the application of the antitrust laws."
Had the decision gone the other way, there would have been a new round of mergers, a key player had warned.

Jonathan Ledecky, president of the business supplier U.S. Office Products, said recently: "If it's approved, I believe it will set off an avalanche of acquisitions and transactions in the office products sectors. Others will want to find strategic partners to keep pace with the size of the industry leader."
